title: Deuda and Gaura: The Culture of the Far West
meta_description: Deuda song and dance and the Gaura festival of Far West Nepal: how they work, when to see them, plus hudke ballads, Masto gods and festival etiquette.
summary: Deuda is the call-and-answer song and circle dance of Nepal's far west, sung by two groups who trade verses for hours. Gaura is the region's great women's festival in late summer, when the goddess Gaura is made from field plants and carried home. Together they are the clearest expression of Sudurpashchim and Karnali identity.

sections.heading: A region with its own voice
paras: Kathmandu sets much of Nepal's culture, but the far west has always had its own. The hills of Doti, Baitadi, Dadeldhura, Bajhang, Bajura and Achham, and the Karnali districts to the east, speak dialects of Nepali so distinct that people from Kathmandu struggle to follow them: Doteli, Baitadeli, Bajhangi and others, often grouped together as the Doteli language. The region's festivals, gods and music are its own too.

For a visitor, the two words to learn are deuda and Gaura. Deuda is the song and dance you will hear at any gathering in the far western hills, from a wedding to a temple fair. Gaura is the festival that turns villages upside down for a week in late summer. Both are living traditions, not performances put on for tourists, and both are best experienced by being invited in.

Politically the region is Sudurpashchim Province, the far western of Nepal's seven provinces, with Karnali Province to its east. Geographically it is a land of steep hills cut by the Seti, Budhiganga, Mahakali and Karnali rivers, with the Terai plain along the south. People here are mostly Khas Chhetri, Thakuri, Brahmin and Dalit communities in the hills and Tharu on the plain. Far from Kathmandu, they have kept customs that faded elsewhere, and many families still divide their year between farming, festivals and work abroad.

sections.heading: How deuda works
paras: Deuda is a song form and a dance at once. Men and women stand in a line or a circle, linking arms or holding hands, and step together in a slow, swaying rhythm, a step forward, a step back, a step to the side. The group is split into two sides. One side sings a short verse, usually a couplet, and the other side answers. The answer must fit the rhyme and the theme, and it should be clever.

That is the heart of deuda: it is a contest of wit. Verses are often improvised on the spot, teasing, flirting, boasting or complaining. A young man may sing to a young woman across the circle, and she replies with a verse that cuts him down to size, to roars of laughter. Older singers recall verses about famine, debt, the forest, the gods or a lost love. A good deuda session can go on all night, with the best singers remembered for years.

Many deuda songs are about separation. For generations men from the far western hills have travelled to India for seasonal work, a journey people call going to Kalapahar. Wives, mothers and sisters sing of waiting for them; men sing of homesickness. Today the destination may be the Gulf or Malaysia, but the songs of parting still carry the same feeling.

sections.heading: Gaura: the goddess comes home
paras: Gaura, also called Gaura Parva, is the biggest festival in Sudurpashchim and is widely celebrated in western Karnali too. It falls in the Nepali month of Bhadra, usually late August or early September, and honours the goddess Gaura, a form of Parvati, and her husband Maheshwar, Shiva. Married women pray for their husbands' long life and the family's wellbeing; unmarried girls pray for a good husband. The provincial government declares a public holiday.

The festival unfolds over several days. On the fifth day of the bright fortnight, women soak biruda, a mixture of five or more kinds of grains and pulses, in a copper vessel. On the following days they go to the fields and shape figures of Gaura and Maheshwar from rice plants, grasses and other crops, dress them in cloth and ornaments, and carry them in procession to a shrine or a house in the village, where the deities are worshipped as guests. Women fast, wear new clothes and tie sacred threads, and the soaked biruda is offered and later shared as prasad.

Evenings belong to deuda. Across the villages women and men dance in long lines around the shrine, singing verses to the goddess and to each other. At the end of the festival the figures of Gaura and Maheshwar are taken out and sent off, much as a daughter leaves her parents' home after a visit, with songs that are both joyful and sad.

sections.heading: Hudke ballads and the Masto gods
paras: Deuda is not the only music of the far west. The hudko, a small hourglass-shaped drum held under the arm, accompanies the hudkeli singers who perform long ballads and dances in the hills of Karnali and Sudurpashchim. Their songs tell stories of local heroes, kings and gods, and were once a key way that history passed from one generation to the next.

Religion in the far western hills is also distinct. Alongside Shiva, Parvati and the gods worshipped across Nepal, villages in Karnali and the far west honour the Masto, a group of local deities, often called brothers, each tied to a particular place. They speak through dhami, oracles who enter trance at festivals and answer the questions of villagers about illness, disputes or rain. Many small stone shrines on hilltops belong to Masto. If you see a dhami possessed at a festival, watch quietly and follow your guide's lead; photography may not be welcome.
Ask your guide which god a village shrine belongs to; the answer often opens a long story.

sections.heading: Changing traditions
paras: Culture in the far west is changing fast. Roads, mobile phones and migration have brought new music and new ideas. Deuda, once a village pastime, is now recorded, released on video and sung at concerts in Kathmandu, and it has become a symbol of far western identity. Young singers mix it with modern instruments, and older singers worry that the art of improvising verses is fading.

Some traditions are changing for good reason. Chhaupadi, the practice of keeping women in separate huts during menstruation, was once widespread in parts of the far west and Karnali. It was declared illegal by Nepal's Supreme Court in 2005 and made a criminal offence in 2017, after deaths of women in cold, smoky huts. Local campaigns, many led by women, have reduced it greatly, although it persists in some areas. It is a sensitive subject; if it comes up, listen rather than judge.
list: Ask before joining a deuda line; you will usually be pulled in with a smile.
Dress modestly at festivals; women may be offered a borrowed shawl or sari.
Do not enter shrines or kitchens without being invited, and remove shoes when you do.
Ask before photographing people, especially women fasting at Gaura and dhamis in trance.
Bring a small gift, such as fruit or sweets, if you are invited into a home during a festival.

faqs.a: Deuda is the folk song and dance of Nepal's far west and western Karnali. Dancers link arms in a line or circle and step together, while two groups trade short sung verses, answering each other with wit, teasing or feeling. Verses are often improvised. It is performed at festivals, fairs, weddings and any gathering in the hills.

Gaura falls in the Nepali month of Bhadra, usually in late August or early September, and lasts several days around the fifth to eighth days of the bright lunar fortnight. The exact dates change each year with the lunar calendar. It is a public holiday in Sudurpashchim Province, so check current dates before you travel.

Women soak biruda, a mix of grains and pulses, then make figures of the goddess Gaura and her husband Maheshwar from rice plants and other crops. The figures are dressed, carried in procession and worshipped. Women fast and wear sacred threads, and evenings are filled with deuda dancing. At the end the figures are ceremonially sent off.

faqs.q: Can tourists join a deuda dance?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Deuda is a community dance, and guests are often welcomed into the line, especially at festivals and fairs. Ask your guide to check first, follow the steps of the people beside you, and do not worry about singing; the verses are in local dialect. Joining in is one of the warmest ways to meet people.

faqs.q: Where can I see Gaura as a visitor?
faqs.a: In almost any village of Sudurpashchim, including Doti, Dadeldhura, Baitadi, Bajhang, Achham and Kailali, and in parts of western Karnali. Towns such as Silgadhi and Dhangadhi hold bigger public celebrations. A village visit with a local guide, ideally arranged through a family, gives the best experience.

faqs.q: What language do people speak in the Far West?
faqs.a: Nepali is understood everywhere, but at home many people in Sudurpashchim speak Doteli and related dialects, such as Baitadeli, Bajhangi and Achhami, which differ noticeably from Kathmandu Nepali. In the Terai, Tharu dialects are common, and in upper Humla people speak Tibetan dialects. A few local words go a long way.

The Masto are local deities worshipped in Karnali and the far western hills, often described as a group of brothers, each linked to a particular place or shrine. They speak through dhami, oracles who go into trance during festivals and answer villagers' questions. Their shrines are often small stone buildings on hilltops.

A hudko is a small hourglass-shaped drum played with the hand, held under the arm. In Karnali and the far west, hudkeli performers sing long ballads and dance to its beat, telling stories of local heroes, kings and gods. Hudke performances are less common today but still appear at fairs and festivals.

faqs.q: Is it respectful to photograph festivals in the Far West?
faqs.a: Public processions and dances are usually fine to photograph, but always ask first when people are worshipping, fasting or in trance, and never use flash inside shrines. Some families prefer that women fasting at Gaura are not photographed. Your guide will tell you when to put the camera away.
